name: Chest/body shaving for gym

lead: Lifters and bodybuilders shave the chest, abdomen and arms so muscle looks more defined, especially in photos and on stage. The effect is visible immediately. Athletes also cite reduced friction and a better fit in tight clothing.
Removing hair exposes the skin surface so muscle contours are easier to see. Methods include razors, trimmers, depilatories and waxing. No studies measure the aesthetic effect.

paras: People shave or trim before photos, shows or beach days and repeat as hair grows back. Some move to waxing or depilatories for longer-lasting smoothness.

Shaving can cause ingrown hairs and irritation. A 2004 study documented an MRSA outbreak on a college football team in which cosmetic body shaving was a facilitating factor, so skin infections in athletes are a documented risk.

angle.text: Shaving the chest, abdomen and arms removes the hair that blurs muscle contours, so definition shows more clearly in the mirror, photos and on stage. The effect is immediate; skin-infection risks in athletes are documented separately.

lead: Chest and body shaving for the gym is the practice of removing body hair, mainly from the chest, abdomen and arms, so that muscle definition looks more visible. Wikipedia notes that bodybuilders and some other athletes shave body hair to highlight muscle development or reduce friction.[1]

Published research on the aesthetic effect is lacking. The medical literature does contain a documented outbreak of MRSA skin infections on a college football team in 2003 that investigators linked in part to cosmetic body shaving.[2]
infobox: Shaving or trimming body hair to show muscle definition

paras: People who shave cite making muscles appear more defined, easier tanning or oil application in competition, and a preference for smooth skin; Wikipedia lists highlighting muscle development, reducing friction and fitting skin-tight clothing as reasons athletes remove hair.[1] Cultural norms about male body hair vary, and the practice is one of the grooming choices discussed in looksmaxxing and fitness communities.

Razor shaving can cause ingrown hairs and follicular inflammation, particularly in people with curly or coarse hair.[3] A retrospective cohort study of a college football team found an MRSA outbreak with 10 cases of cellulitis or abscess; cosmetic body shaving and turf burns were identified as facilitating factors.[2] Clinical guidance for razor irritation generally mentions sharp single-blade razors, shaving with the grain and using a trimmer to keep hair at a short length.[3]
No studies found on the aesthetic effect of body shaving. A related study of infection risk among athletes is described above.[2]

timeline.event: MRSA outbreak on a US college football team in which cosmetic body shaving was a facilitating factor, reported in 2004.[2]
